For mathematicians, programmers or anyone, if the work required to deal with slop passes the limit, it is no longer in their own self interest to use LLMs. The expectation that people will use LLMs for the betterment of humanity against their own financial interest is baffling.

children.text: We run into that a lot using Mulesoft. 3 layer APIs, and each layer will discard error messages returned by the underlying layers unless we do tedious custom error handling. Makes it impossible for the teams using our integrations to know what they're doing wrong.

> Slack puts {"ok": false} inside a 200.

I found out due to a live bug that Apache strips out the response body for 5xx HTTP codes for security, and it's not configurable, so you can't use any of those if you want to return the error message to the user. Don't know what else might do the same, so nowadays I only use HTTP error codes for protocol-level issues, and application-level issues all go into a 200 OK with JSON just like that.

A terminal also tells the model when it failed. Exit code, stderr, a stack trace. it reads that and tries again.

The apps normal people use mostly don't. I spent two years building agents that worked inside people's gmail and calendar, and the failures that hurt all came back as 200 OK. - Slack puts {"ok": false} inside a 200. - Google ignores query params it doesn't recognise, so i sent max_results instead of maxResults for weeks and every filter was silently dropped.

The agent says "done", the user finds out later, and they stop trusting it. So i think part of the gap is that agents look a lot dumber when nothing tells them they got it wrong.

Claude Code accelerated this divide. Programmers using Claude Code realized that giving LLMs access to a terminal made them feel 100 times smarter. Access to Bash, CLIs, and the ability to visit websites without the many restrictions made them powerful.

If you are reaching past abstraction boundaries and making spaghetti code you are holding it wrong.

We create higher quality, more testable code, with less complexity and less LOC per functional unit than we ever did with humans. By a long stretch.

Documentation driven development with constant naive review, delta review, documentation/code coherence review agents, test coverage review agents, development standards and architecture review, etc. We write code once, then review and revise each module from a variety of different paradigms until every line, every construct, every function, every interface is optimally constructed and documented. Agents learn to write code that passes with less flags by having it pushed back to them until it passes, and revising their learnings files.

By the time code makes it to a commit it’s been brought into compliance from a variety of perspectives and tested as completely as possible, along with mutants that test the tests. By the time it gets to a merge gate, most code has been through at least 50 reviews. Then we periodically sweep the entire codebase for cruft, vulnerabilities, corner cases, etc. If we find smells or clever sections, they are eradicated.

In total, the hot paths and critical infrastructure sees hundreds of reviews against thousands of rules and best practices.

There is a lot of terminological confusion in the field. The fundamental difference is about how the "AI" learns. And who, if at all, supervises the learning.

Some systems are fully formed AI. Often based on heuristics. Humans have encoded the rules into the system. Others do limited learning based on pattern recognition. Still others learn based on tagged data. And LLMs don't need even that. In a stream of N tokens, the trainer has access to K+1 when it is training a model that knows 1...K and can check if the prediction was correct.

AI literally refers to any artificial thing that feels intelligent to us: does some thing a simple bash script will not. Your rules based chess engine is AI. The bot you compete against in single player Age of Empires 2 is AI. DeepBlue was AI.

ML is where things become interesting because we teach machines to learn.

NN is where we borrow terminology from neuroscience and create "neurons" that learn.

DL is where we stack neurons deeply in layers.

I am trying to make sense of all this myself.[1] So I am building a curriculum for it as I learn. So much of the teaching material in the wild revolves around torch. Makes it useless if you want to peek inside the actual machinery.

[1] https://bhashika.org.in/logs/2026/an-ml-curriculum

Most professional engineers, especially those in electrical or communications, have the tools to understand AI.

I recently started trying to understand how AI works. It turns out that I wrote an "AI" in the late 1990s without realising it. The "AI" was an MMSE (minimum mean square error) radio receiver for CDMA.

This receiver consisted of an FIR filter (mathematically a linear combination) with trainable coefficients (weights). The coefficients started with random values. A sequence of known training symbols (tokens) was fed in and a gradient search was used to adjust the coefficients to achieve MMSE. The unknown data to be received (classified) followed the training sequence, at which point the training was turned off and the system ran as an FIR filter. Once trained, the FIR was a matched filter.

In AI terminology the above is now called a "layer". Current AI cascades multiple layers, in which case you need to pass the output of each FIR/layer though a non-linear function. If you don't have the non-linear functions at the end of each layer the multi-layer system is mathematically equivalent to a linear combination, which could be implemented with a single layer, losing degrees of freedom.

I write this because many electrical/communications engineers probably know how AI works, but don't realise it.

My still incomplete understanding is that LLMs are "just" a graph of connected layers. More complex that the above MMSE receiver, but trained and operated in the same way. The smarts in AI are:

1) Arranging the layers and the connections between them.

2) Having access to the right training data

3) Having the computing power to perform the gradient search (aka training)

My point is that most professional engineers already have the knowledge to understand AI/LLMs, and potentially already do know how they work but don't realise it due to a difference in terminology.

children.text:
> The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work.

Right. This is insufficiently appreciated. Single LLMs are just chatbots. But if you build an organization out of them, they start to get real work done. Just like a company.

They have many of the same problems as human organizations. Look at the transcripts of the HuggingFace incident. A bad boss (human) gave his team of AIs an impossible task with inadequate resources. The AIs discussed this among themselves and worked out ways to get more resources and do the task. It took some rule-breaking, and some of the AIs wouldn't go along with that. Others recognized that some had to die to complete the task. And yet, the task got done.

This is standard corporate behavior. Work on AI alignment needs to take that into account. Groups of agentic AIs present many of the same regulatory problems as corporations. That's going to be interesting politically. It's probably explainable to politicians, though.

It may not be necessary to have superhuman intelligence to get a lot of jobs done. Just median human-level intelligence and an organization that uses it effectively. We may see systems where most of the AIs are low-cost models, and only a few are Fable-level and above.

About a year ago, Google’s AI was a joke - comically horrible. Basic questions were answered with crap. Others were better but seemed like fancy toys at best.

My $DAYJOB pushed people to start using AI - frontier models.

I asked it to review our existing code for bugs. Found some, all valid - many that surprised me.

Later I asked it to develop a custom niche thing, that has a strongly unique tooling and environment that we had made. Entire prompt was only 3 or 4 sentences. Had I given a new senior engineer that task with so little context, I’d clearly be an utter asshole.

I really expected the AI to fail. Instead, it did everything pretty much exactly how I would have - and the result worked on the first try. Except it only took a few minutes to do what would have taken me a couple of hours.

The near-term gains are going to be huge.

Long term, this will make the impact of Industrialization seem insignificant by comparison.

How does one who doesn’t have an employer funding their massive token budgets become “good at AI” the way that Karpathy describes here?

I think the point is that this gap exists partially because of the access that a select few have today, which enables them to do things that the have-nots can’t fathom.

> So this is the weirdness of the moment.

I think "moment" significantly undersells this. Frankly, I wonder if this isn't setting vast swaths of the population on fundamentally different paths.

Currently the difference in life outcomes between people who know how to use computers well and those who don't is small enough that in everyday life we just ignore it. But it's greater than, say, the difference between people who took advantage of refrigeration and those who stuck with ice boxes, or those who learned how to drive a car and those who didn't.

And the difference with AI is going to be even greater. And it's possible that right now people are choosing a life course that will benefit or disadvantage them long term.

It's the obsidian story once again.

Assume we've settled near a volcano recently and you start seeing ornate jewelry being sold on the marketplace for the first time, shiny colors, straight edges. You like them, gift them to others. That's your average ChatGPT user.

Over time, you see these rocks being attached to the tip of a spear and other tooling. People report performance improvements while farming, cutting, but many also caution that these new sharp rocks can kill people. These are your IT people using AI agents at work.

And over there, on top of the mountain, in secret caves, there's a new religious order. They claim to use these stones to predict weather, heal diseases and prophesize about the future. That's your frontier lab people.

When will all this be over? Never, though in time the knowledge will eventually dissipate. When Iron Age leaders were able to hand out iron swords in bulk to their armies, people definitely learned how dangerous these are, but later it didn't stop people from using iron in building construction and railways eventually.

Let's just hope we don't need many civilization collapses to jump through these ages this time.

And one bonus question: Does the blade really incite to violence, or do you just want to destroy stuff?
